{{Short description|Concept in abstract algebra}}
In [[abstract algebra]], '''cohomological dimension''' is an invariant of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] which measures the homological complexity of its representations. It has important applications in [[geometric group theory]], [[topology]], and [[algebraic number theory]].

== Cohomological dimension of a group ==
As most cohomological invariants, the cohomological dimension involves a choice of a "ring of coefficients" ''R'', with a prominent special case given by <math>R=\Z</math>, the ring of [[integers]]. Let ''G'' be a [[discrete group]], ''R'' a non-zero [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] with a unit, and <math>RG</math> the [[group ring]]. The group ''G'' has '''cohomological dimension less than or equal to ''n''''', denoted <math>\operatorname{cd}_R(G)\le n</math>, if the trivial <math>RG</math>-module ''R'' has a [[projective resolution]] of length ''n'', i.e. there are [[projective module|projective]] <math>RG</math>-modules <math>P_0,\dots , P_n</math> and <math>RG</math>-module homomorphisms <math>d_k\colon P_k\to P_{k-1} (k = 1,\dots, n)</math> and <math>d_0\colon P_0\to R</math>, such that the image of <math>d_k</math> coincides with the [[Kernel (linear algebra)|kernel]] of <math>d_{k-1}</math> for <math>k = 1, \dots, n</math> and the kernel of <math>d_n</math> is trivial.

Equivalently, the cohomological dimension is less than or equal to ''n'' if for an arbitrary <math>RG</math>-module ''M'', the [[group cohomology|cohomology]] of ''G'' with coefficients in ''M'' vanishes in degrees <math>k>n</math>, that is, <math>H^k(G,M) = 0</math> whenever <math>k>n</math>. The ''p''-cohomological dimension for prime ''p'' is similarly defined in terms of the ''p''-torsion groups <math>H^k(G,M){p}</math>.<ref name=GS136>Gille & Szamuely (2006) p.136</ref>

The smallest ''n'' such that the cohomological dimension of ''G'' is less than or equal to ''n'' is the '''cohomological dimension''' of ''G'' (with coefficients ''R''), which is denoted <math>n=\operatorname{cd}_{R}(G)</math>.

A free resolution of <math>\Z</math> can be obtained from a [[free action]] of the group ''G'' on a [[Contractible space|contractible topological space]] ''X''. In particular, if ''X'' is a contractible [[CW complex]] of dimension ''n'' with a free action of a discrete group ''G'' that permutes the cells, then <math>\operatorname{cd}_{\Z}(G)\le n</math>.

== Examples ==
In the first group of examples, let the ring ''R'' of coefficients be <math>\Z</math>.
* A [[free group]] has cohomological dimension one. As shown by [[John Stallings]] (for finitely generated group) and [[Richard Swan]] (in full generality), this property characterizes free groups. This result is known as the Stallings–Swan theorem.<ref>{{cite book|last=Baumslag|first=Gilbert|authorlink=Gilbert Baumslag|title=Topics in Combinatorial Group Theory|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0T4BCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA16|year=2012|page=16|publisher=Springer Basel AG}}</ref> The Stallings-Swan theorem for a group G says that G is free if and only if every [[Group extension|extension]] by G with abelian kernel is split.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gruenberg|first= Karl W.|authorlink=Karl W. Gruenberg|title=Review of ''Homology in group theory'' by Urs Stammbach|journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical  Society]] |volume=81|year=1975|pages=851–854|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1975-13858-4|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* The [[fundamental group]] of a [[Compact space|compact]], [[Connected space|connected]], [[Orientability|orientable]] [[Riemann surface]] other than the [[sphere]] has cohomological dimension two.
* More generally, the fundamental group of a closed, connected, orientable [[Aspherical space|aspherical]] [[manifold]] of [[dimension]] ''n'' has cohomological dimension ''n''. In particular, the fundamental group of a closed orientable hyperbolic ''n''-manifold has cohomological dimension ''n''.
* Nontrivial [[finite group]]s have infinite cohomological dimension over <math>\Z</math>.  More generally, the same is true for groups with nontrivial [[torsion (algebra)|torsion]].

Now consider the case of a general ring ''R''.
* A group ''G'' has cohomological dimension 0 if and only if its group ring <math>RG</math> is [[Semisimple algebra|semisimple]]. Thus a finite group has cohomological dimension 0 if and only if its order (or, equivalently, the orders of its elements) is invertible in ''R''.
* Generalizing the Stallings–Swan theorem for <math>R=\Z</math>, [[Martin Dunwoody]] proved that a group has cohomological dimension at most one over an arbitrary ring ''R'' if and only if it is the fundamental group of a connected [[graph of groups|graph of finite groups]] whose orders are invertible in ''R''.

==Cohomological dimension of a field==
The ''p''-cohomological dimension of a field ''K'' is the ''p''-cohomological dimension of the [[Galois group]] of a [[separable closure]] of ''K''.<ref name=Sha94>Shatz (1972) p.94</ref>  The cohomological dimension of ''K'' is the supremum of the ''p''-cohomological dimension over all primes ''p''.<ref name=GS138>Gille & Szamuely (2006) p.138</ref>

==Examples==
* Every field of non-zero [[characteristic of a field|characteristic]] ''p'' has ''p''-cohomological dimension at most 1.<ref name=GS139>Gille & Szamuely (2006) p.139</ref>
* Every finite field has [[absolute Galois group]] isomorphic to <math>\hat{\Z}</math> and so has cohomological dimension 1.<ref name=GS140>Gille & Szamuely (2006) p.140</ref>
* The field of formal [[Laurent series]] <math>k((t))</math> over an [[algebraically closed field]] ''k'' of characteristic zero also has absolute Galois group isomorphic to <math>\hat{\Z}</math> and so cohomological dimension 1.<ref name=GS140/>
